parts.latex:
Given that $f(x)=\begin{cases}5-(x-3)^2, & x\le 2\\ mx+3, & x>2\end{cases}$

What is the value of $m$ for which $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$?

solutions.latex:
For $f$ to be continuous at $x=2$, the two pieces must agree at $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}5-(2-3)^2&=2m+3\\2m+3&=4\\2m&=1\\m&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A function $f$ is given by the rule

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}(x-2)^2+1, & x\le 2\\ 4x-7, & x>2\end{cases}$$

What is the value of $f\Big(f(0)\Big)$?

solutions.latex:
Since $0\le2$, use the first rule:
$$f(0)=(0-2)^2+1=5$$
Since $5>2$, use the second rule:
$$f(5)=4(5)-7=13$$

3725.stem:
Consider the function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases} x^2-2x+2 & -3\le x\le 1\\ x+1 & 1<x\le 6 \end{cases}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of piecewise function: (-3,17) to (1,1) curve, open circle at (1,2), line to (6,7)

parts.latex: Justify why the function is NOT continuous at $x=1$
Sketch the function for the domain $-3\le x\le 6$.

solutions.latex:
Compare the limits at $x=1$ from each piece.

$$L^-=1-2+2=1$$

$$L^+=1+1=2$$

$$\therefore\ L^-\ne L^+,\ \text{so the function is not continuous at } x=1.$$

criteria: Finds one of $f(2)$ or $f(-2)$ correctly, or equivalent merit
Sketches both pieces with one error, or equivalent merit
Sketches one piece correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A function is defined by the rule

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x + 2 & \text{for } x \ge 1 \end{cases}$$

Which statement is incorrect?

solutions.latex:
For $x \ge 1$, $f(x) = x+2 \ge 3$, and $f(x) = 1$ for $x < 1$.

So the range is $\{1\} \cup [3, \infty)$, not $f(x) \ge 1$.

Statement D is incorrect.

5015.stem:
Consider the piece-wise defined function.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2-1 & x\le 1\\ 4-x^2 & x>1\end{cases}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: marking guideline sketch of the piecewise function with open circle at (1,3)

parts.latex: Sketch the function showing all intercepts.

solutions.latex:
For $x\le 1$, use $f(x)=x^2-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2-1&=0 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
For $x>1$, use $f(x)=4-x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-x^2&=0 \\ x&=\pm2 \end{aligned}$$
But $x>1$, so $x=2$.

$$\therefore\ x=-1,\ 1,\ 2$$
criteria: Finds all 4 solutions without excluding $x=-2$, or finds $x=\pm1$, or equivalent merit

$$R:\ \{y:\ y\in(-\infty,5]\}$$
